unit.title: Promote and up-sell products and services

summary: This unit teaches you to promote the products and services of a hotel, villa or resort in a friendly, honest way. You will learn to know your product, find out what each guest needs, suggest something suitable by its benefits, offer an upgrade or an extra at the right moment, deal politely with a doubt or a 'no', sell alcohol and food responsibly, make simple promotional materials, and record your results.

blocks.p: Every guest who stays at a villa, hotel or resort spends money. Some of that money is already planned: the room, the package, the meal. But guests also spend on things they did not plan, because a friendly member of staff told them about something they would enjoy. That is **promoting and up-selling**. Done well, the guest has a better stay, the property earns more, and you build your own skills and reputation.

This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees. It applies at the front desk, in the restaurant and bar, at the pool, in the spa and tour desk, and even in housekeeping, because every member of staff meets guests. Promoting is never about pressure or tricks. It is about **helping the guest choose well**.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks: a role play at a mock front desk and restaurant table, and the planning and making of a promotion for one product. The assessor watches your manner, your questions, your honesty and your records, not only whether a sale was made.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In all practical tasks use made-up guest names, details and prices. Photograph only the work, never a classmate's face unless the Centre's rules and the person agree.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Promoting means making guests aware of a product or service so that they want to use it. Selling means helping the guest to buy it. In hospitality the two go together: you tell, you suggest, the guest decides.

head: Word
What it means
Example
rows: Promoting
Telling guests about a product, service or offer and why they may enjoy it.
Telling arriving guests that the pool bar has live music on Friday.
Up-selling
Suggesting a better, larger or dearer version of what the guest has already chosen or booked.
A guest booked a garden-view room; you offer a sea-view room with a balcony for a small extra charge.
Cross-selling
Suggesting a different product that goes well with what the guest is buying.
A guest orders curried goat; you suggest rice and peas and a glass of fresh ginger beer.
Suggestive selling
Selling by making suggestions with words such as 'May I suggest...' or 'Would you like to try...'. Up-selling and cross-selling are both done this way.
'May I suggest the pumpkin soup to start?'
Upgrade
Moving a guest to a better room type or category, for extra payment or as a gift from the property.
A repeat guest is moved to a suite at no charge as a treat.
Package
Several products sold together at one price.
A honeymoon package: room, dinner on the beach and a couples' massage.
Add-on (extra)
A small item added to a booking or order.
Late check-out; an extra side dish; airport transfer.

blocks.note: Up-selling is **better or more** of the same thing. Cross-selling is **something extra that goes with it**. If the guest orders a coffee and you offer a large Blue Mountain coffee, that is up-selling. If you offer a slice of rum cake with it, that is cross-selling. Both are suggestive selling.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Why properties want staff to sell

ul: **Sales:** extra sales raise the property's income, which pays wages, repairs and improvements.
**Guest experience:** a good suggestion makes the stay better: a special dinner, a trip to a waterfall, a late check-out after a night flight.
**Repeat business and reviews:** guests who enjoy their stay come back and write good reviews. Reviews matter a great deal, because many guests choose where to stay by reading them online.
**Your own career:** staff who know their product and serve well are noticed, and some properties give bonuses or incentives for good sales.

head: Good selling
Bad selling
rows: Starts with the guest's needs
Starts with what the property wants to get rid of
Suggests something the guest will enjoy and can afford
Pushes the dearest item whatever the guest wants
Gives true facts and the true price
Exaggerates, hides costs or promises what cannot be delivered
Asks once or twice and accepts 'no'
Keeps repeating the offer after the guest has said no
Leaves the guest feeling looked after
Leaves the guest feeling pressured or tricked

blocks.note: Team Jamaica is the training and awareness programme of the Tourism Product Development Company (TPDCo) for people who work with visitors, including those in hotels, villas, attractions, transport and craft markets. Its message is that every Jamaican who meets a visitor is part of the tourism team. Promoting Jamaican products with pride is part of that.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: You cannot sell what you do not know. A guest who asks a question and gets 'I am not sure' or a wrong answer loses trust at once. Good product knowledge lets you answer quickly, suggest the right thing and avoid complaints.

head: Area
What to know
rows: Rooms and villas
Room types, bed sizes, views, balconies, number of guests each sleeps
Which have kitchens, plunge pools or accessibility features
Check-in and check-out times; late check-out rules and cost
Food and beverage
Menu items, how they are cooked, main ingredients and common allergens
Daily specials, sizes, prices, opening times and dress rules
Drinks list: local rums, local and imported beers, fruit punches, sorrel, ginger beer, mocktails, coffee
Spa and wellness
Treatments, how long each lasts, prices, opening hours and booking rules
Treatments not suitable for pregnant guests or for certain health conditions: refer to the therapist
Activities and tours
Pool and beach activities, kids' club, water sports, evening shows
Tours run by licensed operators: what is included, duration, pick-up time, price, what to bring
Packages and meal plans
What is included in each package (meals, drinks, activities) and what is not
Meal plans such as room only, bed and breakfast, half board, full board and all-inclusive
Shop and local products
Souvenirs, crafts, coffee, sauces, rum cake: which are made in Jamaica and where they come from
Prices and tax
The correct price, whether GCT (General Consumption Tax) and any service charge are included, and the rate the property uses

blocks.note: Never guess a price, a time or what is in a package. If you are not sure, say, 'Let me check that for you,' look it up or ask a supervisor, and then tell the guest. Wrong information leads to complaints and lost trust.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Plan
What the price includes
rows: Room only
The room; meals and drinks are paid for separately.
Bed and breakfast
The room and breakfast.
Half board
The room, breakfast and one other meal (usually dinner).
Full board
The room and all three meals.
All-inclusive
The room, meals, drinks and many activities, all in one price. Check what is excluded, such as some premium drinks, spa treatments or off-site tours; these may be sold as extras.

ul: Read the menus, brochures, package details and price lists, and read the daily briefing sheet for specials and changes.
Taste the dishes and drinks when the property allows it, so you can describe them honestly.
Walk through the rooms, the pool, the spa and the restaurant, so you can describe them from what you have seen.
Ask the chef about ingredients and allergens; ask the spa therapist how long a treatment takes; ask the tour desk what is included.
Listen to what guests say about the products and note which ones they like.
Check for changes every day: prices, opening times and out-of-stock items change.

blocks.p: A **feature** is a fact about a product. A **benefit** is what that fact means for the guest. Guests buy benefits.

head: Feature (the fact)
Benefit (what it means for the guest)
rows: The room is on the top floor with a balcony facing west
You can watch the sunset from your own balcony.
The jerk centre uses pimento wood and a slow smoke
The meat has a rich, smoky flavour you will not forget.
The spa offers a 90-minute couples' treatment
You can relax together without having to hurry.
The tour leaves at 7 a.m. from the property
You miss the heat and the crowds, and you do not need to find your own transport.
The kids' club is open from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m.
Parents can enjoy the beach while the children are looked after and have fun.

blocks.note: Say the feature, then bring it to life with 'which means...' or 'so you can...'. 'The room has a balcony' is a feature. 'You can have your morning coffee on your own balcony, looking at the sea' is a benefit.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Finding out what the guest needs

blocks.p: A good suggestion starts with listening. A honeymoon couple, a family with young children, a business guest and a group of friends on a weekend away want very different things. If you suggest the wrong thing, the guest feels you did not listen.

flow: Greet warmly and give your full attention
Watch for clues
Ask open questions
Listen without interrupting
Match a product to the need
Check you understood

head: Clue
What it may tell you
A suitable suggestion
rows: A couple, with a booking note 'honeymoon' or 'anniversary'
They want romance and privacy.
A private sunset dinner on the beach; a couples' massage; a room with a sea view.
A family with small children
They need safe, easy activities and food children like.
The kids' club; a family pool day; a children's menu; a connecting room.
A business guest with a laptop
They need quiet, speed and a fixed schedule.
A quiet room; quick breakfast; late check-out; airport transfer.
A guest who looks tired after a flight
They may want rest and a simple meal first.
Early room if ready; room service; spa later in the week.
A group of friends on a weekend away
They want activities, nightlife and shared experiences.
A boat trip, a group table at jerk night, a cocktail package.
An older guest who walks slowly
They need comfort and short distances.
A ground-floor room; a tour with little walking; seat at a shaded table.
A guest who asks about local culture
They want a real taste of Jamaica.
A licensed tour to a coffee farm or waterfall; Jamaican dishes; a craft market visit.

head: Type
What it is
Example
Use it to
rows: Open question
Cannot be answered with just yes or no; starts with words such as what, how, which, tell me about.
'What would you like to do while you are in Jamaica?'
Find out needs and preferences.
Closed question
Can be answered with yes or no, or a short fact.
'Would you like a table by the window?'
Confirm details and close the sale.

blocks.p: Start with open questions to learn the need. Finish with a closed question to confirm: 'Shall I book the tour for tomorrow at 9?'

ul: Face the guest, keep eye contact and nod. Do not look at your phone or the clock.
Do not interrupt. Let the guest finish.
Repeat the key points: 'So you would like something quiet and not too far to walk?'
Look at booking notes for birthdays, anniversaries and special diets, but keep guests' private details private. Do not say them where others can hear.

blocks.note: Listen for the budget as well as the need. If a guest says 'We are watching our spending,' do not offer the dearest option first. Offer a good-value choice or a smaller version. The aim is a happy guest, not the biggest bill.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Letter
Stage
What you do
Example
rows: A
Attention
Get the guest's attention in a friendly way.
'Good evening! Welcome to our jerk night.'
I
Interest
Link the product to the guest's need.
'You said you love local food. Tonight the chef has fresh jerk pork from the pit.'
D
Desire
Describe the benefits so the guest can picture them.
'It is slow-smoked over pimento wood, so it is smoky and tender, and comes with festival and hard dough bread.'
A
Action
Ask for the decision, with a choice or a closed question.
'Shall I bring you a portion to share, or would you prefer your own plate?'

blocks.h: Good ways to make a suggestion

ul: **Use suggesting words:** 'May I suggest...', 'Would you like to try...', 'Many of our guests enjoy...'. Not 'You need to...' or 'You have to...'.
**Describe in an appetising way:** 'slow-cooked oxtail with butter beans' sounds better than 'oxtail'. Use real descriptions of taste, smell, texture and place.
**Offer a choice of two:** 'Would you like the mango cheesecake or the coconut drops?' makes it easy for the guest to choose and assumes a sale, politely.
**Give the price when it matters:** especially when it is an extra cost. Say the correct price and whether GCT and service charge are included.
**Be specific:** 'a fresh sorrel or a fruit punch' is better than 'something to drink?'
**Smile and use open body language:** a smile, eye contact, relaxed shoulders and open hands. Arms folded and looking away put guests off.

head: Situation
Best time to suggest
rows: Room upgrade
At check-in, before the key is handed over, when you are looking at the booking and the guest is open to ideas.
Drinks at a table
When the guests are seated and before they choose their meal.
Starter or side dish
When taking the main order.
Dessert and coffee
When the main course plates are cleared, not before.
Another drink
When the glass is nearly empty, not when it is full.
Spa or tour
When the guest talks about relaxing or sightseeing, or on the first day so there is time to book.
Late check-out
The day before departure, or at check-in if the guest mentions a late flight.

blocks.note: Suggesting too early (before the guest has chosen) or too late (after the bill) wastes the chance. Suggest when the guest can easily say yes.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Always give the **correct price** and say whether **GCT** (General Consumption Tax) is included. Use the rate your property uses; do not guess a rate.
If a **service charge** is added, tell the guest so the bill holds no surprises. The property's policy sets the rate.
If prices are in US$ and the guest asks about J$, use only the rate your property gives you for the day.
A guest who sees a bill larger than they expected will complain, even if the product was good.

blocks.p: Every department has chances to promote. The best staff know their own chances and also help promote the other departments.

ul: **Upgrades:** check which better rooms are free and what the extra charge is. Offer at check-in, by benefit, with the exact extra cost. Record the change in the booking.
**Late check-out:** offer for a fee, or as a treat for repeat guests, if the property allows it.
**Add-ons:** airport transfer, a welcome fruit basket, a birthday cake, flowers, a spa voucher, a dinner reservation.
**Information:** tell arriving guests about tonight's special, the spa and the tour desk.

flow: Welcome the guests and suggest a drink: a choice of two
Present the menu and mention the chef's specials, described well
Take the order: suggest a starter, a side dish or a larger size; check allergies
During the meal: check satisfaction; offer another drink when glasses are nearly empty
When plates are cleared: suggest dessert, coffee or an after-dinner drink
Presenting the bill: thank the guest; mention tomorrow's special or the Sunday brunch

head: Guest orders
Up-sell (better or larger)
Cross-sell (goes with it)
rows: A coffee
A Blue Mountain coffee or a large size
A slice of rum cake or a pastry
House wine
A better wine by the glass or a bottle
A cheese platter
Jerk chicken
A half chicken instead of a quarter
Festival, bammy and a sorrel
A beer at the pool
A pitcher for the table
Fish fritters or a plate of nachos
Ackee and saltfish at breakfast
A larger plate with fried dumpling and plantain
Fresh juice or Blue Mountain coffee

ul: Offer a premium rum or a signature cocktail instead of a standard drink, but only if the guest is interested.
Offer a mocktail to non-drinkers and to guests who should not have more alcohol.
Promote happy hour, live music nights and bar snacks.
Remember the alcohol rules in the section on selling responsibly.
A guest says they are stressed or have a sore back: suggest a massage by the spa, and describe how it will feel.
A guest asks about things to do: suggest tours run by **licensed operators** and say what is included, how long it takes and the price.
Link products: a spa afternoon for a couple on honeymoon; a sunset cruise with dinner.
A room attendant can mention the spa or the restaurant if a guest asks, leave a promotion card as the property directs, and pass on what guests say.
Gardeners, drivers and security staff meet guests too: they can answer 'Where is the best place to eat?' with a correct, friendly answer about the property's offers.
If you are not in a sales role, you still never give wrong information. Say 'Let me ask the front desk for you.'

head: Product
How to describe and suggest it
rows: Ackee and saltfish
Jamaica's national dish; a hearty breakfast. Suggest it with fried dumpling or roasted breadfruit.
Jerk chicken or pork
Spiced and smoked over pimento wood; suggest festival and a cool drink.
Sorrel, ginger beer, fruit punch
Local drinks. Sorrel is made from the red sepals of the roselle (hibiscus) plant and is especially popular at Christmas.
Blue Mountain coffee
Grown in the Blue Mountains east of Kingston; smooth and mild. A good gift to take home.
Rum cake, pepper sauce, spices
Popular gifts from the shop; check allergens for food items.
Crafts and art
Direct guests to the gift shop or a licensed craft market for genuine Jamaican crafts.
Tours: river, waterfall, coffee farm, cultural sites
Recommend only licensed operators, because they meet safety standards.

blocks.note: Promoting Jamaican products helps guests have a memorable stay, helps the property earn good reviews, and puts money into the community: farmers, cooks, craft makers, drivers and guides. It also supports Team Jamaica's aim that visitors meet the real Jamaica.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Not every guest will say yes, and that is fine. An **objection** is a reason a guest gives for not buying: 'It is too expensive,' 'I do not have time,' 'I will think about it.' A doubt is a chance to help the guest, not a fight to win.

flow: Stay friendly and listen
Ask a gentle open question to find the real worry
Answer honestly
Offer an alternative
Accept the decision
Leave the door open

head: Guest says
What it may mean
A good response
rows: 'That is too expensive.'
The price is higher than expected, or the benefit is not clear.
Listen. Explain what is included. Offer a shorter or smaller version, or a lower-priced alternative.
'I do not have time.'
The guest is busy or tired.
Offer a time that suits them, or tell them the opening hours and how long it takes.
'I will think about it.'
The guest needs time, or has an unspoken worry.
Ask, 'Is there anything I can tell you about it?' Give a brochure or the details, and say how to book later.
'I am not sure it is for me.'
The guest does not know what to expect.
Describe it simply, mention what others enjoy, and suggest a short taster or a smaller version.
'No, thank you.'
A decision.
Smile, thank them, and accept. Do not repeat the offer.

blocks.note: Never argue, sulk or repeat an offer after a guest says no. Repeating an offer after a clear no is **pushy selling**, and it makes guests uncomfortable and less likely to buy anything. A polite 'Of course, enjoy your evening' leaves the door open for later.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Say, 'I will find out for you,' and then do it. Do not invent an answer.
If the doubt is about health (an allergy, pregnancy, a medical condition), tell the guest to speak to the therapist, chef or doctor before booking.
If a guest is upset about a past problem, deal with that first. You cannot sell to a guest who feels ignored.

blocks.p: Trust is the most valuable thing you have with a guest. One lie or one pushy sale can lose it. Selling responsibly also protects guests' health and keeps the property within the law.

head: Rule
What it means in practice
rows: Be honest
Describe products as they really are. Do not promise anything the property cannot deliver, such as a view that is blocked or a tour that is not run.
Give the true price
Say the correct price, and whether GCT and any service charge are included.
Do not pressure
Suggest once or twice at a good time. Accept 'no'.
Check allergens and diets
Before suggesting food, check ingredients with the kitchen. Nuts, shellfish, gluten, dairy, eggs and alcohol in cakes and sauces can all matter. Never guess.
Follow the alcohol rules
The legal age to buy alcohol in Jamaica is 18. If a guest looks young, ask for ID. Do not serve a guest who is clearly drunk; offer water or a soft drink politely.
Recommend only licensed and safe services
Tours, boat trips and transport should be run by licensed operators that meet safety standards.
Respect privacy
Do not say guests' names, room numbers or personal details where others can hear.
Follow the property's rules
On discounts, free items, photos and social media, only do what your supervisor allows.

blocks.note: A guest with a nut allergy asks to try the rum cake you suggested. Do not say 'I think it is fine.' Check the ingredients with the kitchen first, and tell the guest what the chef says. If there is any doubt, suggest something else.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: A guest who appears to be about 16 asks for a rum punch at the pool bar. Politely ask for ID. If the guest is under 18, do not serve alcohol and offer a non-alcoholic drink such as a mocktail or a fruit punch. This protects the young guest and the property.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A **mocktail** (or virgin cocktail) is a drink made without alcohol. Promoting non-alcoholic drinks is good practice: it suits drivers, children, pregnant guests, guests who do not drink and guests who have had enough.

If a guest comes back unhappy because a product was not as you described, listen, apologise and tell your supervisor. Do not blame the guest or argue. Learn from it: describe more carefully next time.

head: Sign of pushy or unwanted selling
Better practice
rows: Repeating an offer after the guest says no
Accept the answer politely.
Talking over the guest
Listen and ask questions.
Making the guest feel bad for saying no
Smile and thank them.
Hiding extra costs
Say the full price clearly.
Offering a dearer product when the guest asked for a cheaper one
Offer good value within their budget.

blocks.p: Promotional materials work for you when you are busy. A good poster or table tent tells guests about a product and makes them want to ask you about it.

head: Item
What it is
Where it is used
rows: Poster
A large printed notice with a heading, a picture and key details.
Lobby, lift area, restaurant entrance, staff notice board.
Table tent card
A small folded card that stands on a table.
Restaurant and bar tables: tonight's special, a cocktail of the day.
Brochure
A printed, folded leaflet describing the property's rooms and services.
Front desk, rooms, tour desk.
Menu and drinks list
Lists dishes or drinks with prices.
Restaurant, bar, room service.
Display
A stand or table showing products, such as gifts or coffee.
Gift shop, front desk.
Social media post
A photo and a few words on the property's page.
Online; only as the property's rules allow.

ul: **What it is:** the name of the product or offer.
**When it is on:** day, date and time.
**Where:** the place at the property.
**Price:** the correct price and whether GCT and service charge are included.
**The main benefit:** one reason to come, in a few words.
**How to book or find out more:** the front desk or tour desk.

blocks.h: Planning and making a poster or table tent

flow: Find out what the product is, who it is for and when it is on
Check the details and price with your supervisor
Decide the main message: name, benefit, day and time, place, price
Write a short, catchy heading and only a few clear lines
Use large, easy-to-read letters and a picture taken with permission
Use the property's colours and logo as its rules say
Check spelling and facts, then get the design approved
Place it where guests will see it, and replace it when the offer ends

blocks.note: A poster that still shows last month's prices is worse than no poster, because it can mislead guests and cause arguments at the bill. If you see one, tell your supervisor so it can be updated or taken down. Keep brochures and displays tidy, full and up to date.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Only post on the property's pages if you are allowed to. Follow the property's social media rules.
If you want to post a photo of a new cocktail on your own page, check the property's rules first.
Never post a guest's face, name or room without permission, and never post anything private or untrue.
Reply to online reviews only if that is part of your job, politely and honestly; otherwise pass them to your supervisor.

blocks.note: Online **reviews** are the comments and star ratings guests write on travel websites. Good service and honest selling produce good reviews. Pushy selling and wrong information produce bad ones.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Every department can promote the others: the front desk tells guests about the restaurant and spa; the bar promotes Sunday brunch; servers mention the tour desk.
When you hear about a birthday, an anniversary or a special need, **pass it on** so the right team can plan a treat. Do this quietly and privately.
Share specials and changes at the daily briefing.
Support each other: if a colleague is busy, offer to answer the guest or take the booking.

blocks.p: Some properties ask staff to record the extra sales they make, on a sales log or the POS. Records show what is working, help plan stock and staffing, and show the property how guests respond.

head: What to record
Why
rows: The product offered and sold
To see which offers are popular.
The number or value sold
To measure against a target.
Guest comments and reasons for 'no'
To improve how the product is described or priced.
The date, time and your name
To check the records and give credit.

blocks.p: A **target** is the amount of sales a staff member or team is asked to reach in a week or month. Targets help people see how they are doing, but they never excuse pressure or dishonesty.

ul: If very few of a new cocktail have been sold after a week, ask guests and colleagues for feedback. Is the description clear? Is the price right? Is it being offered at the right time? Change the approach.
Look at what your best-selling colleagues do: their questions, wording and timing.
Follow up with repeat guests: remember what they enjoyed last time.

blocks.note: Good service makes selling easier. Guests who feel welcome and looked after trust your suggestions. Poor service makes even a good product hard to sell.
blocks.label: Remember

c1.title: Check-in for a honeymoon couple at a villa in Negril
c1.text: Shanice and Andre Bennett, from Kingston, arrive at a Negril villa resort at 2 p.m. Their booking is a garden-view room at J$28,000 a night, with a note saying 'honeymoon'. A sea-view room with a balcony is free for J$6,500 more a night (GCT shown at the current rate). Front desk trainee Odane is checking them in. The couple say they want somewhere quiet and romantic, and Andre mentions he is on a tight budget this month.

c2.title: Dinner service at a restaurant in Ocho Rios
c2.text: Trainee server Kerry-Ann is looking after a table of four: two adults and two children aged 6 and 9. The adults order jerk chicken and curried goat. One guest, Mrs. Patterson, says she has a shellfish allergy. The menu has a fish fritter starter, a rum cake dessert and a fresh sorrel drink. The children have not yet ordered, and the table has no drinks yet.

c3.title: A busy pool bar in Montego Bay
c3.text: Trainee bartender Rushane is working at the pool bar on a hot Saturday afternoon. A guest who looks about 16 asks for a rum punch. A second guest, Mr. Francis, has already had several drinks, is speaking loudly, and now asks for a double rum. A third guest, Mrs. Williams, says she is driving later and just wants something refreshing.

c4.title: A spa package for Mrs. Clarke in Mandeville
c4.text: Mrs. Clarke is staying at a mountain lodge in Mandeville. When trainee Tameka mentions the spa's 90-minute package at J$18,000, Mrs. Clarke says it is more than she planned to spend and that she may not have time. Tameka knows the spa also offers a 45-minute back massage and that a Jamaica Blue Mountain coffee morning at a licensed local farm is available on the tour desk.

c5.title: Promoting Sunday brunch at a guest house in Kingston
c5.text: A guest house in Kingston is starting a Sunday Jamaican brunch from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. at J$3,800 per person including GCT. After two Sundays, only a few guests have booked. The poster in the lobby gives last month's price of J$3,200. Staff have not been told the details at the daily briefing, and nobody records how many guests ask about it.

questions.q: Which suggestion best matches what Shanice and Andre told Odane?
o: A quiet sea-view room with a balcony, described well
The garden-view room, as they asked for the lowest price
A noisy room near the pool bar so they can meet other guests
A table at the restaurant for the night's jerk buffet
questions.why: They asked for something quiet and romantic. A sea-view room with a balcony suits that, and describing what they will enjoy (sunset, privacy) links it to their need.

questions.q: When is the best moment for Odane to offer the sea-view room?
o: After the couple have unpacked and gone to the beach
While he is checking them in, before the key is handed over
When the couple are about to check out at the end of the stay
In a note slipped under the door after midnight
questions.why: At check-in he has the booking open, the room is free, and the guests are ready to decide. Later, the room may be taken or the guests may have settled into the first one.

questions.q: Andre says money is tight this month. What should Odane do?
o: Offer the upgrade again, as honeymoon guests usually want the very best room
Stop mentioning anything extra, since Andre has said that money is tight now
Tell them the price is fixed and that the sea-view room will be given away soon
Give the extra cost clearly and offer a smaller extra, such as a sunset drink
questions.why: Listen for the budget. Give the exact price so there are no surprises, and offer something smaller that still suits a honeymoon. The aim is a happy guest, not the biggest bill.

questions.q: Which of these is a feature of the sea-view room, rather than a benefit?
o: It has a west-facing balcony with two chairs
You can end each day watching the sunset in comfort
You will wake up to the sound of the waves
You can enjoy your morning coffee in the sea breeze
questions.why: A feature is a plain fact about the product: a west-facing balcony with two chairs. The other choices say what the feature means for the guest, which is a benefit. Guests buy benefits, so turn features into benefits when you speak.

questions.q: Before Kerry-Ann recommends the fish fritter starter to Mrs. Patterson, what must she do?
o: Suggest it anyway, as fish fritters are usually made with flour and spices
Check with the kitchen whether it has shellfish in it or is cooked with it
Ask Mrs. Patterson to go and read the ingredients in the kitchen herself
Suggest the rum cake instead, because desserts are known to have no allergens
questions.why: Never guess about allergens. The kitchen knows the ingredients and what shares the fryer, and Kerry-Ann should report exactly what the chef says. Any dish, desserts included, may contain allergens.

questions.q: The table has no drinks yet. What is the best way for Kerry-Ann to suggest them?
o: Would you like the fresh sorrel or a fruit punch to start?
Do you want any drinks at all, or are you fine with just water tonight?
You should all order a drink tonight, as the food here is quite spicy
Everybody at the other tables is already having sorrel this evening
questions.why: Offering a choice of two named drinks is friendly and easy to answer. Closed yes/no questions, pressure and 'everyone else is' wording are weaker or pushy.

questions.q: The adults order jerk chicken and curried goat. Which is an example of cross-selling?
o: Offering a larger portion of jerk chicken for a small extra charge
Offering a better cut of goat that costs more per portion
Offering festival and rice and peas to go with the mains
Offering to move the family to a window table in the lounge
questions.why: Cross-selling is suggesting something different that goes well with what is being bought, such as sides. A larger portion or a better cut is up-selling, the same item made bigger or better.

questions.q: When is the best time for Kerry-Ann to suggest dessert?
o: When the guests first sit down and open the menu
When she takes the main order, so they can plan ahead
As soon as the starters arrive on the table
After the main course plates have been cleared
questions.why: Once the plates are cleared the guests have finished eating and can think about something sweet. Suggesting dessert earlier does not give them a reason to want it yet.

questions.q: What should Rushane do about the guest who looks about 16?
o: Serve the rum punch, as the guest is staying at the resort and is on holiday
Ask for ID, and offer a non-alcoholic drink if the guest is under 18
Ask the guest's parents to say whether it is allowed when they are next at the bar
Give a weak rum punch so that the guest is not served the full strength
questions.why: The legal age for buying alcohol in Jamaica is 18. If the guest looks young, ask for ID, and offer a mocktail or fruit punch instead if under 18. Being a resort guest or having parents' permission does not change the rule.

questions.q: Rushane has refused Mr. Francis another drink. Mr. Francis becomes loud and argues. What should Rushane do?
o: Pour a small drink to calm him down, then refuse any more after that one
Argue back and explain the law to him until Mr. Francis finally agrees
Stay calm, repeat the refusal politely and call his supervisor
Ask the other guests at the pool to persuade Mr. Francis to leave the bar
questions.why: Stay calm and polite, do not argue, and get help from the supervisor or security if the guest will not accept the refusal. Giving in or arguing makes it worse and puts the guest and others at risk.

questions.q: Mrs. Williams is driving later and wants something refreshing. What is the best suggestion?
o: A mocktail made with fresh fruit and ginger beer
A rum punch with only a little rum in it
A light beer, as it has less alcohol than rum
A frozen cocktail, because the ice makes it weaker
questions.why: A mocktail has no alcohol, so it is safe for a driver and still special. Any alcohol, even a small amount, is a risk for someone who will drive.

questions.q: Mrs. Clarke says the package costs more than she planned to spend. What should Tameka do first?
o: Say that the price is already a special one and that it cannot be changed
Tell her that all the other guests have already booked the same package
Listen, then offer the 45-minute back massage as a smaller option
Say she will have to decide at once, because the spa is almost fully booked
questions.why: A price worry is an objection to deal with, not a fight. Listen, then offer a smaller choice that fits her budget. Inventing pressure such as a full spa is dishonest.

questions.q: Mrs. Clarke says, 'I will think about it.' What is the best response?
o: Offer a brochure, tell her how to book later, and thank her
Ask her to sign up now and cancel later if she changes her mind
Say the offer will be gone by tomorrow so she must decide
Say nothing, and walk away because she has said no
questions.why: Give her what she needs to decide in her own time and leave the door open. Pressure and false deadlines damage trust, and walking away without helping misses a chance to serve.

questions.q: Mrs. Clarke tells Tameka she has high blood pressure. What should Tameka say about the spa?
o: Not to worry, as all spa treatments are good for everybody who comes in
That she should ask the spa therapist about her health before booking
That the spa does not take any guests with health problems at all
That she should take her medicine and then book any treatment she likes
questions.why: Health questions belong to the therapist or doctor, not to a sales assistant. Tameka should never guess whether a treatment is safe.

questions.q: Why is the licensed coffee farm tour a better suggestion than an unlicensed driver who offers the same trip for less?
o: Licensed operators always charge the lowest prices of all the tour firms in the area
Licensed operators have to include a free meal in every price they charge
Licensed operators run all of their tours at exactly the same time every day
Licensed operators must meet safety standards, so it is safer for the guest
questions.why: Properties recommend licensed operators because they meet safety and service standards. If something goes wrong, the property's name is attached to the recommendation.

questions.q: Why is the poster in the lobby a problem?
o: It shows a price that is not the price the guest will be charged
It uses too many colours and so is hard for the guests to read
It is placed in the lobby, where guests are not likely to be looking
It gives the time of the brunch, which should be kept private from guests
questions.why: A poster with an old price can mislead guests and cause arguments at the bill. Staff who spot it should tell the supervisor so it can be corrected or removed.

questions.q: Staff have not been told the brunch details. What is the main effect on selling?
o: Staff will sell more, as they feel free to make up details
Staff will only sell to repeat guests who already know the offer
Staff cannot give correct answers or suggest it with confidence
Staff will refuse to take any bookings for the brunch
questions.why: Good product knowledge is the base of selling. Staff who do not know the time, price or what is included cannot answer questions, and guessing leads to complaints.

questions.q: What is the most useful thing the guest house could record about the brunch?
o: Only the total money taken at the end of the day, whatever it was spent on
How many guests asked, how many booked, and why some said no
The names of the staff who did not mention the brunch offer to guests
How many guests ate breakfast at the guest house on each of those days
questions.why: Records of enquiries, bookings and reasons for 'no' show whether the problem is the price, the wording or the timing, so the approach can be changed. The aim is to learn, not to blame staff.

questions.q: A guest orders a regular coffee. The server says, 'Would you like a Blue Mountain coffee, or a regular one with a slice of rum cake?' What is happening?
o: The server is up-selling and cross-selling
The server is discounting the coffee in order to get more sales from the guest
The server is dealing with a complaint about the coffee from the guest
The server is promoting a competitor's product to the guest by mistake
questions.why: Offering a better coffee is up-selling; offering cake with it is cross-selling. Giving a choice of two also makes it easy for the guest to decide.

questions.q: A guest asks the price of a spa treatment. You only remember last month's price and a poster shows an older one. What do you do?
o: Quote last month's price to the guest, as it is probably still the same
Quote the price shown on the poster, since the guest can see it too
Give a rough price and say that it may change a little when the bill comes
Check the current price list, tell the guest and report the old poster
questions.why: Give only the correct, current price and say whether GCT is included. A wrong price causes arguments at the bill. Report out-of-date posters so they can be corrected.
